subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT THOMPSON COMMISSION INQUIRE INTO EFFECTS OF OIL TANKER TRAFFIC IN STRAITS OF GEORGIA AND JUAN DE FUCA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely, marine traffic in oil and other hazardous cargo along the west coast of Canada. In view of the fact that Dr. Andrew Thompson indicated yesterday that he is anxious to continue his investigation under the Public Inquiries Act into the marine and environmental risks of west coast tanker traffic, and in view of the fact that the abandonment of the Kitimat proposal may result in substantially higher volumes of tanker traffic in the Georgia Strait and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen):
That the Thompson Committee, under the Public Inquiries Act, be instructed to continue its investigations and, if necessary, that the inquiry's terms of reference be amended to permit it to shift its emphasis from the Kitimat area to the Strait of Georgia and the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF ALLEGED ACTIONS OF GOVERNMENT WHICH HAVE ERODED TRADITIONAL THINGS OF OUR HERITAGE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a question of urgent and pressing necessity in connection with the tinkering by this government with the things of our heritage by administrative action, as it has endeavoured in the last few years to change the statutory name of the national holiday on July 1 from Dominion Day to Canada Day, and the present anticipated change in the capital city of Canada, which would require an amendment of the British North America Act, which provides that Ottawa shall be the capital. Such actions constitute an affront to parliament and are a denial of the basic principles of the rule of law under the constitution. I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That a committee of both Houses be set up to look into and report on the step-by-step erosive action that is being taken, not by parliament but by the government of Canada, in the whittling away by surreptitious means the traditional things of the heritage of our country and to put a stop to it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ENSURE PRESERVATION OF LANGUAGE RIGHTS OF QUEBEC INUIT-POSSIBILITY OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister and it arises from the profound concern that the Inuit of northern Quebec have about their right to use freely either official language-a right which is part and parcel of the James Bay Agreement which was passed only last month by this House. Despite extensive negotiation with the Quebec culture minister, Camille Laurin, the Inuit have failed to obtain the written guarantees of exemption from the provisions of Bill One, which I would respectfully suggest they have a right to expect. My question to the Prime Minister is this. Has he or any of his ministers contacted the Quebec ministers and spoken to them directly and frankly about this parliament's determination to ensure that the language rights of native people are preserved?

Mr. Speaker, may I put a supplementary question to the Minister of National Defence. Can the minister explain to the House why it took three hours for the National Defence search and rescue helicopters based in Gander to be dispatched to the scene? The search and rescue request went from St. John's to Gander at 9.10 p.m. The helicopters did not leave Gander until midnight and they arrived over the site at 2 a.m. This meant that a number of the survivors from the ship which sank at 10 p.m. were on the ice that length of time and could have lost their lives.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN DISPATCHING HELICOPTERS TO SINKING "WILLIAM CARSON"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reaction time was less than was expected for the helicopters to get on the scene. There were not only two Labrador helicopters from Gander but an Argus and a Buffalo aircraft from Summerside, all of which arrived about the same time, plus the helicopter from the Canadian coast guard ship Sir Humphrey Gilbert. There were also six Sea Kings alerted from Summerside, two of which had reached Gander and there was a further Hercules on alert.
The reaction was very fast, taking the flying time into consideration. Forty-two people were evacuated by armed forces helicopters and 80 by the Canadian coast guard helicopter onto the coast guard ship. The whole operation moved very smoothly and was a classic example of cooperation between the various departments, particularly the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence. I think great credit goes to the skipper, Captain Hinks of the William Carson who handled the situation with calmness and maintained calmness on board. All the rescue gear was in working order and the ship rescue team operated with a high degree of efficiency.

member referred is being conducted by the federal-provincial task force formed to identify areas of unacceptably high radioactivity across the country, particularly those affecting work places and places where people live. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in April the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the government's intention to co-ordinate appropriate and festive activities to celebrate and honour Canada's federal national holiday on July 1. The decision was prompted by the growing number of expressions of national unity from groups and associations across the country and the recognition of the impressive number of July 1 projects and activities being initiated by communities across Canada.

We all remember that in 1967, millions of Canadians joined together to reaffirm their pride in their country. Since that time, the federal government's July 1st program has been centered in Ottawa with regional activities being left to the initiative of local groups and municipalities. I want to ensure that the momentum which began in 1967 is revived and maintained in future years. We hope to provide a permanent framework for a well-structured, decentralized national program within which groups and individuals across Canada may express, in their own way, their pride and belief in Canada. [English]
To date over 1,000 communities have begun preparations for activities which will reflect their recognition and pride in Canada. A national community program is providing all the planning assistance possible to these communities through consultation, promotional support and co-ordination. With the government's co-operation, each activity will be the communi-
Dominion Day Celebrations
ty's expression of national pride. Viewed together, these initiatives will express the diversity that makes Canada so unique.
We are working in close co-operation with the Council of Canadian Unity, a national association which has organized Canada Week since 1969. When Canada Week was launched in 1969, some 50 Canadian communities participated. So far this year, 1,000 communities have initiated their own special projects.
We have also asked the private sector to participate in this national effort. The response to that has been enthusiastic. Several major companies have come forward with offers to help promote the July 1 celebrations across Canada, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has made available its regional offices to assist in the co-ordination of the activities being undertaken.
We have also established two specific programs to support our national effort.

A major campaign will be launched over Canadian radio and television expressing the government's conviction that Canada Day is a day for celebration and pride. The theme of the English campaign is "Canada, I want to shake your hand" and the French theme is "Le Canada, un beau pays, un pays libre". The two themes are appropriate ways of reaffirming the country's size, beauty, and the freedom which Canada allows for self-expression, growth, and diversity.

We will also assist Canadian celebrities to travel throughout the country with their families to participate in regional events and meet as many community residents as possible. Many well-known Canadians have expressed an interest in participating in this program. Within a few days I should be able to announce a list of their names.

On July 1, the CBC will carry a three hour special television spectacular, in English and French, featuring local and national celebrities in a national view of the Canadian Mosaic. Private network tie-ins will expand the viewing audience to an estimated 6 million people.

While we are placing our major emphasis on our national celebration from coast to coast, Ottawa will be the site of a special day of festivities, including a parade of original floats depicting Canada's history and diversity. The trooping of colours will be presented the morning of July 1, and beginning at 1 p.m. Ottawa will celebrate the Great Canadian Birthday Party, a giant five-hour festival of folk dancing, music, sports, children's activities and contests. The Great Canadian Birthday Party is being organized by a volunteer citizen's committee with our support and assistance. I know members of parliament from the Ottawa area are vitally interested in it.
The climax to the Ottawa festivities will be a three-hour spectacular on Parliament Hill featuring English and French

June 3, 1977
Dominion Day Celebrations
performers and celebrities from across the country. In keeping with the objective to decentralize the Canada Day celebration, live performances from across the country will be included by satellite in the CBC's three-hour special. The Ottawa Spectacular will be tied in to the CBC television program so that Canadians across the country will be able to enjoy it. A giant fireworks display will follow the Parliament Hill program, bringing to an end what promises to be a most exciting celebration of Canada's federal national holiday.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of my party are happy to celebrate the anniversary on July 1. I am anxious to respond without a series of platitudes because these festive occasions bring on the worst in public speaking. I am not accusing the minister. As a matter of fact, I thought his statement was rather happily spared in this regard. I am anxious to avoid the platitudes, the hucksterism and the boosterism. What we want is a happy birthday shared by as many Canadians as possible. I have to be thankful for what we have in our common citizenship.
1 do not think we should be disturbed about the preoccupation of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) concerning the heritage aspects of what others have struggled to give us to celebrate. The technology of television will mean Canadians will celebrate in their own way. The smaller places in Canada to which the minister referred will be drawn together because of the focal point of the nation's capital. I am anxious to see whether the partnership of Radio Canada and the CBC will work out arrangements to celebrate this day together. It would be an interesting test if all Canadians could see the same things on July 1.
I do not know what it is about the English Canadian psyche which makes them rather reluctant to get emotional about celebrating patriotic events. I am sure it is part of our psyche. Every once in a while we surprise ourselves. We did on July 1, 1967. Suddenly, English Canadians found they were able to be moved by exemplifications of our nation and found themselves caught up on Parliament Hill in what was a very moving and emotional experience. It was an experience which I will never forget because it was a family day. I hope family days will prevail across the country.
A wise Canadian of international recognition from Toronto, Northrop Frye, told us about this endless search in which Canadians are engaged. Occasionally we seem to have the elusive thing we seek. I must agree with what Northrop Frye said, that if we stop the search and look around, we will find the Canada we have. I hope that will be part of our celebration.
Perhaps I will be categorized as being unspirited arid Scrooge-like. I do not intend that at all. I hope the birthday will be a tremendous success. We have to face the fact that half the people who have not worked on this July 1 celebration are the young. This is not the time to mention what we are going to do about this. It will be a concern of every one of us as we set off the fireworks and troop the colours. We have to

remember that too many young Canadians may be wondering what it is they have to celebrate.
I am looking at an hon. friend across the floor, who will remain unidentified. As Canadians celebrate their birthday, they might recall that years ago it was Her Majesty the Queen who commented upon patriotism in Quebec. I may be considered inelegant because I am going to attempt to paraphrase what the Queen said, which is probably inappropriate. In Quebec, the Queen said that patriotism may take on different dimensions and we should not be surprised if everyone does not have a common expression of patriotism. I thought that was a wise observation. People make lists about the way other people celebrate their citizenship. We do not need any lists, and we do not need any Brownie points for our mutual feeling in regard to our country. It is divisive if we watch others celebrating our national holiday.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party I should like to express our appreciation of the efforts which are being made for a great celebration on our one hundred and tenth birthday on July 1. It is true that there are times when celebrations and ceremonies can be so much window-dressing. There are times when patriotism is known to be a refuge for certain kinds of persons. However, it is also true that there are occasions when celebrations, ceremonies and expressions of patriotism do something for people such as those who comprise this country.
There is no question but that the efforts that were put into celebrating our centennial ten years ago gave us a lift. Sometimes we are a little unhappy that that experience seemed to die down a bit. Now that we are at the point of celebrating 110 years in the life of this country, I think it is worth while that it be done in the thorough way that has been announced by the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts).
I am sure that we all approve of the two-faceted approach, namely, that celebrations are to take place all over the country in hundreds of different communities, and also that there will be a main, outstanding celebration here in the nation's capital. I note that the Secretary of State indicated certain plans for the celebrations on that day. I particularly support the suggestion of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) that an effort be made to see that it is a family day. Not only are we a Canadian family, but we are made up of our own families.
It is appropriate that the performers who take part that day in the main represent the two principal groups in this country, French-speaking and English-speaking. However, I would like to suggest, if it is not too late, that the program might also include performers who represent other groups in this country. There are millions of Canadians who are neither Frenchspeaking nor English-speaking in their origin. They should be represented as well, and let us also remember the natives who are descended from those who were here before any of us came. It strikes me it would be a more Canadian program if this mosaic approach were included in that ceremony. I am
June 3, 1977

delighted to see the Secretary of State nodding his head vertically as I make that suggestion.
One other question does get mention from time to time in this connection. I note what the hon. member for Fundy-Royal said about it. May I say in passing that the issue that arises when we seem to be going to celebrate Canada Day and Dominion Day on the same day could be resolved very easily if the government would just call Bill C-30. That bill provides for the establishment of Heritage Day. It also provides for changing the name of July 1 officially from Dominion Day to Canada Day. Two or three members of the Progressive Conservative party have presented their own bills calling for that change. There is a good deal of support for the idea around this House. Surely in the days between now and July 1 that problem could be solved in that way.
Like the hon. member for Fundy-Royal, I feel this is a celebration which should be enjoyed for its own sake. We should be grateful for the things that are part of our heritage. However, I cannot help but feel that a way to make Canadians even more proud to be part of this country is to put much more effort into solving some of the problems that face us at this time.
The previous speaker referred to the unemployed in our midst, particularly the large number of young people who are unemployed and who will have some doubts about their appreciation of their heritage. A way to make sure that Canadians will forever be proud to be Canadians and want to celebrate our birthdays year after year is to deal with problems like unemployment, urban renewal, regional disparities, housing and all those things that are realities in our life.
For the older people there is the whole question of improving the security that we provide for them, as well as providing those who are working with a guarantee that as they get older their security will be enhanced. Obviously, when I get into these few headings I could make full-dress speech on the things that are of concern to me. However, I am satisfied just to mention them at this time. I am glad to see the Secretary of State nodding his head up and down. I trust this means he agrees that the best way to make sure we will celebrate our birthdays with enthusiasm, not just with palaver and ceremony, is by making Canada the kind of place in which we are not only proud to live but in which there is security and freedom as well as the opportunity for fulfilment for all our people.
We are happy to join with other members of the House in expressing our appreciation of the efforts being made to provide a real "bang-up" celebration on July 1 when Canada will be 110 years old.

most unfortunate that the French version I received was written in very poor French; the text was full of mistakes, both spelling and syntax, when Parliament has in fact excellent translators, who do terrific work. One need but read Hansard to realize how true what I am saying is. That such a text should have been received from a minister, and more, the Secretary of State for Canada, is unforgivable. I therefore trust that he will attend to that inexcusable anomaly on his part, no malice intended. Once again, I feel things must be brought out into the open if improvements are to be made.
The Social Credit Party of Canada supports the idea of a big celebration for Canada. It will be and must be Canada's day. I insist on this because in these days we must of necessity be proud of the fact that our country bears the name of Canada. So, the name must be repeated very often and I trust that celebration will truly be that of the whole of Canada, from the Pacific to the Atlantic.
We deplore, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State and thus the government, and perhaps also Parliament, have as usual once again waited till the fire is roaring before calling firemen. For 10 years now we have been telling this government that Canada is in bad shape, that the provinces are dissatisfied, that Quebecers are beginning to be fed up with what is going on, that the government is sitting by while the economic and social situation is getting ever more rotten to such an extent that there are now over one million unemployed people in our beautiful and great country, when there is so much to do and all those energies that could be used.
In his statement, the Secretary of State has mentioned that prominent people would travel throughout Canada. He told us a few minutes ago that in the next few days he will announce who those people will be. I think it would be normal that travel expenses be paid not only for prominent people-who could afford to pay their own way-but also for little people, unemployed people and Quebecers who do not know much about Canada. They should be given a chance to travel throughout Canada. It would serve our country very well if more Quebecers could visit the other provinces. This is a suggestion which, I hope, will be considered.
In 1967, there was a great boom for the centenary of Confederation. Then everything was dropped or nearly so because, as mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last April, separatism in Quebec is dead indeed. At that time, the Prime Minister thought it was over. By the way, I would like to draw the attention of the Secretary of State to a situation I witnessed on Monday, May 30, in my riding on the occasion of the launching of a book to celebrate the third centenary of a municipality along the St. Lawrence River. The person in charge of the press conference criticized us because the federal government had refused to help Financially in the preparations for this event. And of course, as a member of Parliament and as a Canadian, I reacted. I was not very happy to hear that the organizers of the festivities had presented a project under the Canada Works program to try to organize something good and that the project had been turned down. Mr. Speaker, you imagine that a member of parliament who

has a heart and whose blood boils in his veins, would propose to bring this to the attention of the authorities at the first opportunity. This is what I am doing, and I would ask the Secretary of State to remember this, because a tricentennial does not happen every day. So there ought to be a policy across Canada to help celebrate those days in all provinces of the country.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister stated that separatism was dead in Quebec. I think he must have found on November 15 that his prediction did not quite reflect reality, but something must be done to solve the problem. We must take action, and in taking action, we must do something which will show all Canadians, in any province, that Canada is governed by a Parliament and a government which responds to the needs of all Canadians and want to give all Canadians an equal opportunity to share the wealth and revenues of the country.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I would say to Parliament and to the government that something has to be done most urgently. I want also to stress the fact that our confidence in the present constitution, as well as that of Canadians at large, will erode progressively. We will thus realize that there are people in Canada who really want to work together, who understand each other whatever the language and who want to make Canada the most beautiful country in the North American continent.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night at the time of adjournment I was discussing Bill C-26, and particularly the impact which it will have on the granting councils and university research. I gave some indication of what I felt lay ahead, some of the directions which I felt were implicit within the bill. I concluded my remarks last night by suggesting that I feel that the bill itself is timely and that it would be a vehicle for some important evolutionary changes within the functioning of the granting council system-a system which, I might add, historically has served this country extremely well.
Now I would like to look at another part of the framework of the granting councils which exists outside granting councils itself but which I have discussed both in committee and on second reading. I am referring, of course, to the role of the

Inter-Council Co-ordinating Committee. This committee, as I indicated on second reading, will report to me. It will consist of the Secretary of MOSST, as chairman, and the heads of the three councils. It will be the forum for discussions among the councils and between the councils and the government. It will have as a prime function the job of co-ordinating the policies, programs and practices of the councils, to see that, on the one hand, they do reflect national objectives and priorities, and on the other that they make sense from the point of view of the universities for the development of university research across the range of disciplines. The councils have, of course, final responsibility for shaping their own objectives and supporting policies and programs. This is quite clear. The ICCC will be the sounding-board for discussing their completeness and consistency and their total impact on the university research community. This will be a new and significant element in the federal granting picture.
The ICCC will have other functions. It will advise on the allocation of funds among the councils; it will take an active role to ensure that the needs of interdisciplinary research, both within councils and crossing the boundaries of both disciplines and councils, are met; it will try to see that all disciplines are covered. The committee can invite others to its meetings from both outside and inside the government. As the new councils become established, I can see that the ICCC will be a valuable forum for looking at the interaction and balance among departmental programs of university support and council programs, for example, those of agriculture and the new natural sciences and engineering research council. There has been criticism that the ICCC is not in the bill and, without statutory authority, will lack muscle. In my view that is not so. Its authority derives essentially from the intention the government has for it, its membership and its role. Its scope and action remain flexible and, as with the bill, the concept behind its creation is evolutionary change.
I have laid emphasis on the need for clearer objectives for research support by both the councils and the universities themselves. I noted in my second reading statement the kinds of objectives, in broad terms, the councils might be guided by. I would like briefly to elaborate on certain of these, because I would like the House to appreciate the longer term implications of this bill and the importance of what will be done here today in bringing this bill a step closer to final approval. I would also like to feel I have the support of the House for the thoughts I am putting forward.
The goal of all university research must continue to be excellence assessed by the peer review system, whether it is in unravelling the structure of an enzyme or in developing new techniques for extracting oil from tar sands. I have said, however, that the era of all university research being motivated solely by the desire to expand the frontiers of knowledge is passing. Research in the universities is now multifaceted, and increasingly the stimulus for the research will be coming from outside the university. But we cannot expect, as a nation, that university research will be able to contribute fully to national
June 3, 1977

issues if we do not define what the research objectives are with respect to those issues and what opportunities there are for university scientists and scholars to get involved.
The challenge to the new councils is to develop policies and mechanisms which will encourage the university research community to respond. The problems posed to the community should not only be those of direct concern to governments and industry, as I indicated last night, but should also cover the issues confronting Canadian society in general. The broad objectives or guidelines I described last December provide a context for the definition of these research objectives. To speak in particular of two of them, I think the councils must consider a regional balance of scientific capability and the support of interdisciplinary research in setting out and implementing their objectives. The objective of achieving a regional balance should not be interpreted as meaning that the government wants to see a regional balance within each discipline. This would be unreasonable; we simply do not have the resources. What is intended is a fair distribution of centres of specialization in different disciplines or groups of disciplines across the country. Thus, we should reinforce a regional capability which has grown out of the presence of an outstanding scientist or scholar or a special competence related to the geographic, economic or social conditions of the region.
There will be difficult decisions for the councils here on what to support, and where. The appropriate marshalling of talent and resources in centres of specialization will depend on a detailed knowledge of the state of the art in various fields of research and an understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the universities, including an awareness of the attitudes to research of the university administrations. The councils must begin to obtain this information if they do not already have it.
The councils should also, I believe, give serious thought to how interdisciplinary research is best supported and carried out. Some success has been achieved by the present councils in supporting scientists and scholars from different disciplines working together in various university institutes which cut across traditional departmental lines. From my own observations, I know, however, that many of these efforts have been tentative and have failed to develop the right kind of institutional mechanism or reward systems which would ensure continuing success. There are obstacles in the way of establishing the mutual respect necessary for good teamwork. These will have to be overcome if the optimum level of research capability in Canada is to be achieved. Future progress in addressing national problem areas will be based on the sharing of knowledge among disciplines, as will the general advance of knowledge, and new policies and programs from the councils will be needed. It is especially in these areas that bright, young scientists would be able to pursue research careers.
It is not difficult to think of areas of national concern where research is essential. The efficient development of our agricultural and food technologies, the management-including both exploitation and protection-of our marine resources, the identification of poisons in our atmosphere and water affecting the
Scientific Activities of Government health of Canadian society, and the increasing concentration of Canadians in a few urban centres are examples. The councils, bearing in mind provincial and regional priorities, will have the task of translating national issues into research objectives.
What will these research objectives look like, and how will they be arrived at? I am not sure I can answer this question with any assurance. This will be a task for the councils. It has not been done to any extent before, but what is clear to me is that it will require leadership from the councils to see it through. The process of setting these objectives must, I think, have the involvement and support of the scientific and scholarly communities. Without the backing of the community, the response to such new objectives is not likely to be of high quality or quantity. The challenge, as I say, will be for the councils to come up with policies and programs which strike the right note. I would add that universities themselves may also find their research policies have to be re-examined in light of the changing directions of council programs.
Finally, I do not want to leave the impression that the councils will be devoting all their resources to specific issues. The support of free inquiry has a firm place in council objectives and, as I emphasized, will continue to have that place. Basic research has produced much of the knowledge underlying our present prosperity. Canada will go on contributing to that body of knowledge which is the common property of all mankind. To be a parasite on this stock of knowledge is not the government's policy. Our contribution has been distinguished in the past and I hope it will be even more distinguished in the future.
I have not spoken today about the other aspects of the bill. They were discussed previously and it was agreed in the committee that they would be useful and worth-while changes. I would simply like to conclude my remarks by reiterating my thanks to all hon. members of the House who participated in the discussion on this bill. I would cite two in particular, the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) and the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) who took a very particular interest in this bill at second reading, through the committee stage and on to third reading. I am very grateful to them and the other members of the committee who participated in the debate on this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few remarks I would like to make in this third reading debate. I hope to conclude by one o'clock. The concerns I expressed about Bill C-26 at second reading are in the main still with me. At the time of the second reading debate I said I believed that by putting in place an additional layer of bureaucracy, the net amount of money available for actual research would be less. Given the illusory position of the government with regard to reducing the cost of administration, and given the constraints placed on total budget estimates, we can only conclude that there will be, by the mechanism of this bill, less money available for actual research, where the real work is done. However, as the minister has said, some of this

June 3, 1977
Scientific Activities of Government may be redressed by re-examination by the university community of the projects on which they are working.
Further, I was somewhat concerned about the release on April 26 by the minister regarding the contracting out of scientific requirements to the private sector. In effect, that is merely a reshuffling of the deck. The existing policies of the government for industrial research are, in real terms, available to only 5 per cent of Canadian industry, and they really should be oriented to 95 per cent. Only about 1,550 Canadian firms are capable of supporting in-house research and development. Another 5,000 Canadian firms are capable of purchasing research from private or provincial research foundations. The balance of about 24,600 Canadian firms can neither support in-house research nor purchase research on new products from private or provincial research foundations. The basic problem is that the government has never committed itself to the establishment of a strong secondary industrial base in Canada. I see little, if anything, in this legislation to change that.
Elowever, it is not our purpose to frustrate this legislation on that point. We do not intend to prolong the debate on that point. We will pursue it through other legislation to try to effect a change. In his book "The Economics of Industrial Innovation" published in 1974, Professor Charles Freeman said the following:
No amount of improvement in education and quality of labour force, no greater efforts by the mass media, no economies of scale or structural changes, no improvements in management, or in government administration could in themselves ultimately transcend the technical limitations of candle power as a means of illumination, wind as a source of energy, or iron as an engineering material, or of horses as a means of transport. Without technical innovation, economic progress would cease in the long run and in this sense we are justified in regarding it as primary, although operating in close association with other factors.
The very basis of a manufacturing industry is the systematic application of science and technology. Technology is the key to industrial progress and the key to competitive survival. Appropriate technology is the key to the development of small, regional enterprises in the less developed regions of this country. Much of that appropriate technology should be geared to the resource bases of those regions. Most of our legislation is geared to the development of economies of scale and of specialization agreements and exclusion from monopoly legislation in order to achieve those economies of scale.
The criticism I have is that the base is being continually narrowed and little attention is paid to broadening it. For this reason we were critical of the transfer of the patents and development branch to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, where we believe it will be lost in the bureaucratic jungle and will wither on the vine. We believe there is a mechanism whereby the patents and development branch could act as a clearing-house for patents from other jurisdictions that have run their course and become public property. We believe these should be made available to Canadian enterprises through the libraries of provincial research foundations. On some of this proven technology, new technology can be

built and innovative enterprises spawned that will provide the products of the future.
Canadian industry is suffering from extreme fragmentation such as the proceedings at GATT and the proposal to reduce tariffs generally by 50 per cent across the board, and further fragmentation will take place. I do not oppose tariff cuts if we put in place mechanisms to develop new and appropriate technology geared to regional requirements. Without this commitment, however, the immediate future for industry is indeed very bleak. The future for the 1.5 million unemployed and those entering the labour force in the years ahead looks dark. The possibility of a reversal in our balance of payments deficit is not promising.
Most of the points I have made could have been included in this bill, but they have not. The criticism I have of the bill is not so much on its content but that it could have gone further. It could have incorporated many of the points I have mentioned and taken a bold, new direction for Canada.
I do not view science and technology in any partisan way. It is too important to be pushed into the background by political bickering. The representatives from the scientific and academic community who visited our offices while this bill was being debated brought with them their sincere concern for the future of scientific research. They stressed very conclusively the need for continuous funding so that they could keep their research teams together. They talked sincerely and with conviction about their concerns for future scientific research and the need for long-term funding so that they could continue to attract the best students into this vital field. I can only say to them that we appreciate their concern and will endeavour to address ourselves to it in the months ahead.
I urge the scientific and academic community not to give up because of the constraints on spending we presently face. The short-term future may look bleak, but the long-term future is bright. To those who are being enticed away by promises of higher rewards we say, "Pause and think about the future of Canada". The difficulties we face will be of short duration in the span of an academic life, but we need the very best minds that are available if we are to achieve the promise of the future.
Mr. Speaker, the debate on this bill was spirited, and that is good. The committee hearings were extensive, and that is good. By agreement, we have decided that the bill should pass with a minimum of debate at this stage because of the earlier debate and the depth of the committee hearings. I believe that is good, too. Our desire now is to conclude third reading debate so that the bill may pass through the next stage and be proclaimed. Whatever benefits may accrue to the scientific and academic community should be made available to them as soon as possible.
One of my colleagues said that this bill is one whose time has passed. That is his opinion. An opinion does not have to be right or wrong in order to be valid; it need only be honest. That was his honest opinion and he was perfectly right to express it. That is the nature of debate; that is part of the function of parliament. We endeavour to improve legislation presented to
June 3, 1977

this House so that the final product will be useful and relevant to Canada. Although we have reservations about this bill which we have expressed in debate and in committee, only the passage of time will prove or disprove our reservations and concerns about the effectiveness of the legislation. I, personally, hope that the concerns and criticism 1 have expressed are wrong. I hope that whatever benefits may flow from this bill will give the direction so desperately needed in this field.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we in this party look forward with anticipation to new initiatives that may be presented to this House to enhance and strengthen scientific research and technical innovation in Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the minister in whose name the bill stands cannot be present in the House this afternoon. Let me say, as I begin my comments, that I support the position the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) took on second reading. Juggling around with the granting mechanism and establishing new granting councils will not solve our difficulties in scientific research. The new granting body may employ more people than the old council, but that will do little good. After all, unless you make more money available for scientific and social research, cutting the pie up into smaller slices will not increase its over-all size.
Scientific Activities of Government
I was amazed, to say the least, at some of the things the minister said this morning. He said, for instance, that the government does not intend this country to be a parasite on other countries in the field of scientific research; that is not government policy. Also, he said Canada will do its share. That is precisely our position. In a study carried out for the Ministry of Science and Technology in 1975 it is stated:
-major capital stock of any industrially advanced nation is not its physical equipment but rather its body of scientific knowledge and the capacity of its population to use this knowledge.
According to Statistics Canada we are now turning out about 2,500 Doctors of Philosophy a year, the largest number ever. Again according to Statistics Canada it is unlikely, given the policies we have been following in the research field, that as many as half of their number will be able to find gainful employment. That is a disaster for the country and a tremendous waste of our human and financial resources.
What are the reasons for our deficiency in technological capability? It seems to me there are two: first, with the encouragement of the government and, indeed, of four governments since the Second World War, we have been too willing to import prefabricated, American technology. This is primarily the result of Canada having the highest dependence of any industrialized western nation upon foreign controls and ownership of its industry. As many scientific researchers have pointed out, in most multinational corporations the major research and development effort takes place in the country where the head office is located. Although subsidiaries do perform research and development work, a large portion of this work is adapted, consisting of taking products and processes designed by the parent company and adapting them to the Canadian situation and environment. Clearly, if Canada continues to depend upon the scientific and engineering skills of other countries the long-term consequences will be disastrous.
The minister said he did not want us to be parasites. But if he would look at the figures for research and development he would see how far we have fallen behind in recent years. Public support of research and development in Canadian industry, in government laboratories and in universities has been steadily falling off since 1969. In 1975, support of industrial research and development dropped to 87 per cent of the 1969 level. Support of government research and development fell to 83 per cent of the 1969 level, and of university research and development to 67 per cent of the level in 1969. Is it any wonder statements have recently been made by the Royal Society, by medical researchers, by the Chemical Institute and by virtually every scientific body in this country expressing alarm over the situation?
I suppose that because of the close relationship between the medical profession and the people they serve, it is the medical researchers who have been most successful in persuading the government to make up, at least partially, for the mistakes of recent years. These cutbacks, the scope of which I have indicated, were further aggravated by the termination of such programs as the Industrial Research and Development Incen-

June 3, 1977
Scientific Activities of Government
tives Act, by cutbacks in the program for the advancement of industrial technology and the elimination of the research granting activities of the Defence Research Board. In contrast, other advanced nations like the United States, Britain and France treated their research and development enterprises in 1974 either as well as they did in 1969 or better. The Royal Society commented in its statement last year that Canada appeared to be alone among the advanced nations in the attitude of its government toward research and development.
The second reason for technical weakness can be traced directly to our poor record of support for university basic research. A significant aspect of this neglect is the apparent deliberate attempt by the government to scuttle university research completely, as documented by the Royal Society in the statement to which I have referred. There has been a dramatic decline in the funding of basic research at Canadian universities. Funding by the National Research Council, in real dollars, in 1974 dropped to 60 per cent of the 1969 level, and by the Medical Research Council to about 80 per cent of the 1969 level. As I say, as a result of representations by medical researchers and others this situation has been rectified to the point at which this year we should be giving about the same amount to medical research as we did in 1969.
The proportion of the gross national product spent by the federal government on basic research through its two main funding agencies has been steadily decreasing since 1969. In that year it was a meagre .10 per cent; by 1969 it was .07 per cent. In contrast, Belgium spent .3 per cent; Germany .3 per cent; France .4 per cent; Japan .4 per cent, and the Netherlands .6 per cent. In other words, Canada spent about one-quarter of the average support level of those West European countries and Japan. We are talking, it should be remembered, about a country which until recently, at least, had one of the highest gross national products of any in the world.
In 1974, Canada's increase over the 1969 support level amounted to between 8 per cent and 10 per cent, whereas in West Germany it was 150 per cent, in France 100 per cent, and in the U.S.A. 50 per cent. In the United Kingdom, which we know to have been suffering serious economic difficulties, the increase was 60 per cent. Unlike Canada, these countries clearly recognize that basic research capability provides the underpinning for future technological development, resulting in a strong secondary manufacturing section with its high growth of employment opportunities.
We have seen a continuing decline in recent years in the percentage of our labour force engaged in manufacturing. We have increasingly become hewers of wood and drawers of water. This is a serious matter because there is evidence that the United States may be revising its strategy of allowing unimpeded export of expertise and know-how to Canada, or to other nations, for that matter.
In a paper to the congressional subcommittee on economic growth in 1975, Robert Gilpin, a Princeton economist, warned of the dangers to American leadership in science and technolo-

gy and to the American international market position. He said that if one is to acquire foreign technology, one must have technology with which to bargain and trade. If the United States government were to follow the advice of Mr. Gilpin, there is no country in the world which would be more adversely, indeed disastrously, affected than Canada since we depend almost exclusively upon the United States for industrial knowhow. To a tremendous extent this know-how is imported into Canada from the United States.
It seems to me that in our present weak position Canada has two choices. We can continue to plead for special status with the United States, or we can begin to move toward being technologically independent. To my mind there is no difficulty in choosing the better policy for Canada to follow. But if we are to follow the objective of becoming more technologically independent, we must recognize the necessity for a strong base for technology and then initiate a science policy which commits this country to the furtherance of this objective.
It seems to me very obvious from the figures that I have quoted, figures which have been made public through the work of all scientific organizations founded in various fields in Canada, that this government has not followed such a policy. Indeed, the government has an anti-science policy. It would be charitable to say that this can be ascribed to the lack of understanding of the value and role of science as a moulding force of society. If anyone feels that 1 am being too harsh when I say that, 1 would refer them to the view of a former minister of science and technology, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), that all scientific organizations felt that way. Really, nothing has changed since that time.
The Senate committee headed by Senator Lamontagne which studied at great length and over several years scientific research made a number of interesting observations. In the second volume of its report it had this to say:
A second feature of basic science that justifies financial support is that it is not as pure as it is often alleged to be. Indeed it would be quite easy to show that many important innovations since the first industrial revolution have originated from basic research and scientific discoveries that were not at first viewed as having practical application. The financing of such research can thus be rationalized on the basis that basic science be considered as an overhead charge on applied science and R and D in general.
This government is taking exactly the opposite view. It has taken the view that we have a limited amount of money for scientific research; that therefore cutbacks will be made on pure science and basic research grants. There will be cutbacks in funds for universities and more money will be spent on the practical application of scientific research. As I say, this is the converse of the observation in the Lamontagne report. The Science Council, in their report, had this to say:
It is generally accepted that research is an indispensable element of a university for the development of both teacher and students. Thus Canadian education requires research in Canadian educational institutions. Research at the universities need not and should not be limited to basic research alone. Nevertheless, the search for new and deep understanding of the world which is inherent in basic research make it particularly important to higher education.
Clearly, the opportunity for original inquiry helps generate new knowledge, is an important adjunct of professional teaching and is central to the education of advanced students.
June 3, 1977

Today, a majority of new graduates in virtually every scientific discipline in Canada simply cannot find jobs in Canadian universities, in the government service or Canadian industry. The task force on research reported in Science Forum, in one of this year's issues:
-if the current policies and enrolment trends persist we must face the prospect of a period of 20 years during which few posts in research and teaching will be filled by young recruits. Thus the research work continues to be deprived of fresh talent, and would age rapidly (at an estimated rate of 0.8 years per annum). Continuing erosion will lead to a major crisis in the 1990s when the majority of the present researchers will be of retirement age without adequate replacement of their expertise being available f-om within the country.
That is what has been happening in this country, and we believe it ought not to happen, that it need not happen. 1 come back to what I said at the beginning, that the restructuring of the granting agencies will have very little effect on what we accomplish in the field of scientific research. The prime reason for our failures has been, is, and will continue to be, lack of adequate funding. We believe we must commit at least four-tenths of 1 per cent of our gross national product to scientific research. We agree that the agencies and the government organizations which are charged with approving scientific research projects and granting money should be simplified. This is why we support this bill as a first step. However, we believe that without a sharp increase in the amount of grants we will continue to fail, as we have been failing in the last ten or more years.
We believe that the agencies need to be charged with the responsibility of sponsoring more of what has been called, in the scientific community, mission-oriented research. This is research which may involve a considerable element of basic research but which nevertheless is directed toward a specific goal or mission. This type of research is most often conducted in a government or private research institute. Many countries, particularly France, West Germany and the Soviet Union, have promoted these research institutes with considerable success. We have experimented with this type of research organization in the establishment of Atomic Energy of Canada, Limited which was largely responsible for the basic research and development which led to the CANDU nuclear reactor which we claim is one of the best in the world. Unfortunately, there are a few other examples in Canada of this type of research organization which might best be called a research and development corporation.
We are facing a dilemma. On the one hand, there is a growing surplus of manpower in the science and engineering fields, with little indication of what we should do with these people; on the other hand, funding for research and development has steadily decreased in terms of constant dollars over the last ten years. Hence, fewer and fewer jobs are available for our graduates.
I am suggesting an institute for the establishment of a solar energy research and development Crown corporation. I understand the United States is in the process of establishing such an institute. Such an institute could not only conduct research
Scientific Activities of Government on solar heating and cooling of buildings, solar cells, solar fuels, etc., but could also co-ordinate all solar energy research activities in Canada. The world is crying for the use of solar energy. The industrialized countries, and particularly the underdeveloped countries, are not likely in the foreseeable future to have the funds for alternative energy sources or to have the funds to purchase oil, natural gas, coal or any of the other existing sources of energy.
Canada should take the lead in not only meeting its own needs in 10 or 20 years from now through the use of solar energy but in developing a basis for using solar energy in ways which could be exported to the benefit of Canadians and to the benefit of recipient countries. I am referring to a system for tapping the solar energy available. This is one example of the many we ought to be exploring and about which we have done virtually nothing.
As I have indicated, Canada ranks far behind other industrial countries in their percentage of gross national product devoted to research and development. When we look at applied research and development, largely carried out in industry, Canada ranks last out of eight industrial countries in the percentage of the research and development dollar devoted to industrial research. It was less than 40 per cent in 1972. Not only is the quality of research and development conducted by industry in Canada very poor, but also the quality appears to be poor. It has been discovered that of the 110 significant innovations in the world since World War II, which cover a wide range of science intensive industries including electronic components, pharmaceuticals, plastics, computers, etc., none was first developed in Canada. Although this study covers the period to 1970, recent data suggests that we have not been doing much better since then.
Compared to most other countries, industry in Canada provides a higher percentage of the funds for industrial research and development as compared to the United States, for example, where research and development is the most intense and industry provides a smaller proportion of the financing than in other countries. The government must participate with industries to share the financing of industrial research and development through direct grants and cost-sharing programs, particularly in industries which will help build a secondary manufacturing base and allow diversification from dependence on resource-based industries which we have had in recent years. The secondary manufacturing base in Canada has been deteriorating. The success of these shared ventures will depend on clearly identifying projects which are geared to the special needs of the Canadian market. That will not happen as long as this country continues to be dominated, particularly in the manufacturing sector of our economy, by the multinational companies.
The ability of this country to function as an independent nation will depend on our capacity to develop a strong secondary manufacturing industry based on products and ideas developed from a heavy investment in research and development. This must come from the government. It may be too old-fashioned to talk about Canadians being hewers of wood and

June 3, 1977
Insurance Companies
drawers of water. As one scientist said, the only thing that has changed has been to replace the axe by the chain-saw, and the pail by the water-pump.
In our view, we need a national science policy designed to promote scientific and technological innovations to meet the important economic, environmental and social challenges confronting us and to enhance our daily lives. To achieve this we need a government willing to commit a much greater percentage of our gross national product to basic applied research and development. We need research and development Crown corporations to help these national goals. We also need a firm commitment by the government that we are going to move to regain control of our industry in order to stimulate this applied research and development.
Science is too important to continue in the way we have. While we support the bill we have before us, we do not believe the government really means to do the kinds of things in the field of scientific policies which are required. We foresee much more trouble in the coming years than we have had in the last couple of years, with more unemployment and more difficulties for the thousands of graduates we have been turning out from our scientific institutions.

subtopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO CLARIFY DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
that Bill S-3, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill relates to three types of companies-Canadian companies, Commonwealth companies, and insurance companies from other parts of the world. The main purpose of the bill is to revise the existing statutory rules concerning the valuation of the liabilities and assets of insurance companies and concerning the presentation of accounts. The objective of these changes is to have the financial accounts of insurance companies presented in a manner that will conform more closely to generally accepted accounting principles than has been the case in the past. These matters have been under intensive study for the past two or three years, stimulated by the accounting profession in Canada and in the United States and also by the Canadian Institute of Actuaries.
The problem of fair presentation of financial accounts of an insurance company is a difficult one. The valuation of a company's obligations involves elements of judgment relating to whether policies will give rise to claims in the future and

when these claims will arise. On the assets side, it is necessary to form a judgment concerning the earning power of the existing assets portfolio and whether this portfolio, together with future investment income and future premium payments, will produce the right amounts of money at the right time to pay future claims and expenses. Thus, the valuation of the liabilities and the valuation of assets for an insurance company are closely linked.
A further difficult problem relates to the fact that administrative expenses in connection with the issuance of insurance policies are heavily concentrated at the outset of the policy. It has been traditional in the insurance industry to treat these acquisition expenses as an outright expense as they are incurred. However, standard accounting practice would, instead, spread the impact of the heavy acquisition expense over a period of years rather than concentrate it at the outset. The traditional practice has been conservative in the sense that a company is forced to have sufficient resources to carry this initial expense while it waits for recovery of the expense from future premiums. On the other hand, the standard accounting approach gives, perhaps, a better ongoing assessment of the financial results of a company's operation.
In proposing these amendments, the government recognizes that it is not only desirable to revise and improve the presentation of financial accounts of insurance companies but that it is also desirable to retain sufficient safeguards to protect the solvency of such companies. It is also considered desirable to arrive at one statement form for use by supervisory agencies, as well as for presentation to shareholders, policyholders and the public, if this can be achieved. We recognize, too, that changes from the traditional method of presentation of accounts to methods that are more closely in line with generally accepted accounting principles will take some time. Further thought and development of ideas are certain to take place. The existing bill would amend the present legislative structure in order to permit a revised presentation of accounts and also contemplates some flexibility to take into account results of future and ongoing discussions among the interested parties.
With respect to liabilities, the bill proposes considerable changes from existing requirements. There will be much more responsibility placed upon the actuary of a life insurance company to choose appropriate valuation bases and valuation methods. There will be broader scope than at present to spread the impact of acquisition expenses over the premium-paying period of the policy, thus producing a better presentation of the profit or loss of a company from year to year.
With respect to regulatory control, the bill proposes that the Superintendent of Insurance shall have final control to reject valuation bases that he thinks are inappropriate, and the bill also proposes a maximum limit on the deferral of acquisition expenses.
With respect to assets, the bill proposes that a company be able to present its assets at the book values, less an investment valuation reserve to be determined by regulation. The book
June 3, 1977

values, in general, will be defined at the amortized values for redeemable securities, and the outstanding balances for mortgage loans. For stocks, the book values would be the purchase price together with a special adjustment applied to the whole portfolio, to recognize some portion of realized and unrealized capital gains and losses. Real estate would have a book value equal to the purchase price.
It is proposed to fix the investment valuation reserve by regulation since there is considerable ongoing discussion in the accounting and actuarial professions concerning appropriate methods to value assets for insurance companies. There will likely be further developments in this field from time to time in the future. We would wish, however, to discuss these proposals with the industry before final decision. Draft proposals have been distributed.
For property and casualty insurance companies, although much of the above applies, the bill proposes a change in the minimum capital and surplus requirements now prescribed for this type of company. These changes should help to improve the capacity of existing insurance companies to serve the Canadian market but without any dangerous weakening of solvency standards.
One change of interest is that the bill proposes a change in the definition of "British company" in order to extend this definition to include organizations such as Lloyd's of London. At present, Lloyd's is exempt from the application of the insurance legislation since it is not a "corporation" and the act presently deals only with British organizations that are corporations. Lloyd's has expressed some interest in being registered under federal legislation. In the past, this has not been possible since Lloyd's could not find a way to deposit assets in Canada to cover their liabilities in Canada, as is required of other non-resident insurers. It now appears, however, that Lloyd's has made an arrangement to deposit assets in Canada and, consequently, it seems possible to work out arrangements to give them registered status.
However, some further discussions are needed since the Lloyd's organization has characteristics that are not found in ordinary insurance companies. Consequently, the bill proposes that this change come into force only on proclamation. It also proposes that authority be given to the Superintendent of Insurance to work out special arrangements to meet the special nature of the Lloyd's organization, all within the concept of maintaining assets in Canada to cover the liabilities here.
The bill proposes a modest increase in corporate powers of insurance companies to enable them to transact ancillary business directly, rather than only through subsidiaries as at present. Some additional flexibility will be given to insurance companies to permit them to issue capital stock in classes or series of shares and to subdivide the par value of shares. In this connection I might mention that it is the intention to propose a general revision of the corporate clauses of the insurance legislation as soon as this can be done. In the circumstances now facing us, however, this further revision will probably await completion of the studies of the Bank Act and, perhaps, legislation relating to other financial institutions.
Insurance Companies
The bill proposes a number of changes with respect to investment powers. The power to invest in government securities other than those of governments in Canada will be restricted to government securities of countries where a Canadian insurance company is doing business, but the bill proposes that the government bonds of other countries may be authorized by regulation.
Since the bill received first reading in this House, the question of depositing foreign pay securities to cover Canadian liabilities has assumed greater importance. Because of certain accounting rules adopted in the United States a number of companies from that country have indicated a desire to deposit U.S. dollar securities in Canada to cover some or all of their liabilities here. It seems necessary, therefore, to have broader control over this matter than was originally thought necessary. Accordingly, it is proposed to amend the bill to make clear that a non-resident company may deposit or rest in trust securities not payable in Canadian dollars only with the consent of the minister and subject to such conditions and such valuation as he may prescribe. The provision now in the bill relating only to government securities of the home jurisdiction would then be unnecessary.
When the bill received attention in the other place there was no objection raised. The insurance industry indicated that it was satisfied with the amendments. However, since that time a number of comments have been received, mostly from the investment community, concerning the revision of the investment provisions. These comments were not critical of the principles involved but sought some revision of technical details to ease the problem of determining eligibility of new issues. It seems reasonable to make changes to accord with such requests. Consequently, some amendments will be proposed in committee to that end. In addition, a few other drafting points have been called to our attention and these also might be corrected in committee.
This is a bill of some technical complexity. The Superintendent of Insurance and other officials will be readily available to the committee for the purpose of considering this revision.

subtopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO CLARIFY DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister indicated, this bill has come to us from the other place where it was passed on March 16. Essentially, as the minister also said, it is a housekeeping bill with certain improvement provisions in it. I want to refer to the proceedings in the committee of the other place for a moment where the bill was referred to by the Superintendent of Insurance as being a formidable looking document, although he pointed out to the members of that committee that it was not quite as bad as it looked. I am not sure that he should be considering legislation on the basis of how it looks, but it is a fact that the bill has essentially three parts with basically similar provisions applying, first to Canadian companies, second to British companies, and third to foreign companies. So it is really only the first 17 clauses that we will be considering as the important part of the content.

Insurance Companies
I think the minister made the point that the main purpose of the bill is to revise and clarify the requirements for financial reporting for insurance companies. Reference is made in the bill to the use of actuaries and the studies that have been made by the actuarial societies and the accounting bodies, including undoubtedly the Institute of Chartered Accountants in Canada. I am often reminded that most people think of accounting as being an exact science, and I always disagree with that. I think this is a good example to show us that accounting is, in fact, an art. This amendment indicates that there are, in fact, many ways of presenting the accounting story, particularly in the insurance industry, and the bill will try to give some consistency to the presentation of the financial statements of insurance companies. I think we can all be thankful for that because it is not every individual, whether he be an investor or a policyholder, who can pick out the differences in the various shapes of the presentation that are possible at the moment.
I think it is a particularly good idea that the method of writing off expenses will be standardized. It used to be, in the insurance business, that a new insurance company was limited in the amount of business that it could write. On the one hand, most new companies want to do as much business as they can because that is a sign of activity and, usually, profitability. In the case of insurance companies, because of the write-offs that they were required to do, the case was the opposite; the more business they wrote, the more money they lost in the beginning, and they had to wait until the business first on the books had matured and started to produce some revenue before they could carry on and write more business.
It is an illustration that we might compare with the pipeline companies, for instance, or any other manufacturing concern where the initial investment, while it is very large, is set up on the books as a capital asset and is not written off until the revenue is earned. The practice that has been followed in the insurance companies is that the initial expenses of acquiring a business, such as sales commissions, and so on, have been written off, causing early losses on paper.
I note, also, that the proposals in the bill will give insurance companies broader powers in the field of real estate. That may, or may not, be a good thing. I want to examine a few avenues on that score. They have the power now to invest in real estate, subject to certain limitations. The proposals here would make two or three changes. In the first place, the companies would be enabled to invest jointly with other corporations in other real estate projects. I think that is something that would be acceptable-it would spread the risk a little bit.
Secondly, they would be able to invest in any one parcel an amount of 4 per cent instead of 2 per cent, of their total assets. I would like to comment on that in a little more detail because I am not sure that is not one of the areas with which we should be very careful in the House. Legislation such as this is designed to protect the policyholders more than the shareholders, and if these insurance companies, which have vast amounts of dollars to invest but very low shareholder equity,

June 3, 1977
relatively speaking, are enabled to double the amount they can invest in any particular parcel, then the exposure is being doubled to the shareholders-and that is all right-but also to the policyholders because, with the low equity ratio per shareholder, the policyholders are not far behind.
Already the insurance companies have embarked upon practices which I question, and I hope the committee will look at them when the bill gets to committee. That is, they have adopted the practice of buying land for development, and instead of developing it they lease it on a long-term basis to developers. Then the developer needs a mortgage loan, and normally he goes back to the same mortgage company and borrows on the mortgage on the property from the same insurance company. So, in effect, the insurance company has either total, or very nearly total, ownership of that development although it is subject to a leasehold of, usually, 65 years-sometimes longer, and sometimes shorter. There are two objections to that practice. First of all, any loss of equity in a particular project will reflect back on the equity of the shareholders, and if that is not adequate, the loss goes back to the policyholder. The object of the legislation is to protect the policyholders.
The other objection to which we must be alerted is that the insurance companies, by doing this, become the competitors of the ordinary developers and the tendency then, because there are then additional demands made on the purchase price of land, is to inflate the price of land and, once the project is completed, to deflate the rent. Members of the House may say there is no danger in investing in real estate-it is always going up. I would like to remind them of three cases that have been important enough to come to the attention of the House recently involving taxpayers' dollars. They were instances where the government-owned Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, because of enormous losses in projects, was forced to foreclose and take back possession of these projects. Undoubtedly there will be a tremendous loss-in one case it has already been realized-to the government and, therefore, to the taxpayers.
Those three instances are, first, the Rochdale loan in Toronto which was sold by CMHC at a great loss; second, the Hamilton Place project in Hamilton, Ontario, on which the government has had to commence foreclosure action and nothing has happened to the development for two years and it stands incomplete with something like $7 million or $8 million of taxpayers money invested and earning nothing; and third, right here in Ottawa the Quai d'Orsay which also is under foreclosure by CMHC. So I think that is a danger which we must look at very carefully.
I want to look quickly at the bill. The defintions do not really require any comment. I do not think the minister mentioned the investment by the insurance companies and securities of governments of countries other than Canada and the provinces. I think that when we get into committee we can find out why countries such as Australia and the United Kingdom, to name a couple, are no longer to be allowed as investment securities by insurance companies.
June 3, 1977

I think the changes in eligibility of common shares are reasonable. Instead of having a complete dividend report every five years, one of the four preceding years can be missed; in other words, four out of five.
There is another matter which I do not think the minister mentioned but which bears some careful consideration. Clause 9 would require certain companies to appoint a valuation actuary. When we get into the committee I think we will find out about that. I suppose the following clause is consequential. It would permit the auditor of a company to rely upon the opinion of the valuation actuary. I am not sure what the present process is, but I think we will have to be very careful with this, particularly because we have had problems with auditors and Crown corporations relying on outside auditors. Complications like that led to the introduction of Bill C-20, the Auditor General legislation, which is presently before the committee.
With those few reservations we on this side are generally in agreement with the proposals before us. We hope this bill will get to the committee quickly and that the committee will give it due consideration.
