speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) cannot be here today, so I am going to take his place.
We have before us today a bill which presents itself as a unique and innovative vehicle for law reform. It addresses a problem common to all systems of legislation, namely, the existence of minor inconsistencies, anomalies, and other errors which have developed as a result of the process of passing the 400 or 500 statutes currently in operation at the federal level.
The special quality of this bill is, as I have said above, found in the manner in which it has been developed. Some time ago an announcement was made of this process of non-controversial law reform, and concerned members of the public were invited to submit appropriate suggestions to the Department of Justice. In response to this announcement a number of submissions were received from members of the provincial bars, from members of the judiciary, and from individuals whose positions

June 3, 1977
Statute Law Amendment Act
gave them a working understanding of various acts of parliament. In addition to organizing these suggestions, the Department of Justice also undertook its own study of where this kind of minor change was needed. A draft bill was then prepared, which was given to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for consideration. As befitting the nature of the bill, the valuable contributions of the members of the committee were made and accepted on an entirely non-partisan basis, and the bill before us today is the result of the committee's unanimous agreement. I might add that the committee also endorsed this special process for efficient enactment.
Before completing my remarks, I should emphasize that although this is the first time such a bill has come before parliament, it is our intention to develop an ongoing process for this kind of reform. To that end in the name of the Minister of Justice I again invite interested parties to forward to the department any other possible amendments of this nature.
In conclusion, I simply ask hon. members on all sides of the House to finalize this commitment to this important technique of law reform, and thereby meet our shared responsibility to provide Canadians with the most accurate legislation we can produce.
As the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) has mentioned, it is my understanding that there would be unanimous consent to deal with all stages of this bill today. I hope unanimous consent will be granted so that Bill C-53 can be referred to the Committee of the Whole House rather than to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (for the Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
subtopic: DIPLOMATIC AND CONSULAR PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH IMMUNITIES AND PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
that Bill C-6, respecting Diplomatic and Consular Privileges and Immunities in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, having first entered the public service 15 years ago as a member of the Department of External Affairs, it gives me nostalgic pleasure to present this bill to the House on behalf of my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson).
The purpose of the legislation is relatively simple and I think I can explain its essential nature very easily. It gives the effect of statute law to two international conventions-the Convention of Vienna of 1961 and the Convention of Vienna of 1963. The first is a convention with regard to diplomatic relations and the second is a convention with regard to consular relations. The legislation places the existing and customary international law on a statutory basis within Canada. In other words, the provisions which this law places in statute form are

already binding on the government as the common law standards of international law. In a sense what we are doing is codifying the existing situation and to some extent elaborating it in greater detail. It will make more specific the existing obligations placed upon the government by virtue of its membership in the international community.
I can assure hon. members that this legislation gives no greater immunity or no more privileges to diplomatic or consular officials than they hold at the present time. It will, however, make it easier for Canada to apply present standards of international law since the material will now be easily available to those who need it in a definitive form. The legislation, then, is not very controversial and I hope hon. members will expedite its passage to committee.

subtopic: DIPLOMATIC AND CONSULAR PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH IMMUNITIES AND PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just because this is a Friday afternoon and an occasion on which a good deal of business is being transacted does not seem to me a reason why a bill having certain implications should be quickly handled, particularly when the opening statement by the minister is more significant for what it has omitted than for what it has contained.
I wish to spend a few moments discussing the bill. I ask myself: why has it been brought forward at this time? It is true, as the minister has told us, that the bill presents us with nothing new, to the extent that the Vienna Conventions of 1961 and 1963 have been adhered to by Canada as well as by most of the other nations of the world, and that what is now codified in the measure before us does not in any way change the rights or immunities which our diplomats in other countries enjoy or which we ourselves extend to diplomats who come to Canada. The purpose of the bill is to put into statute form certain of the articles in the two Vienna Conventions. I believe we ought to ask ourselves, when the bill goes before the committee, why certain other articles in those treaties have been excluded.
As the minister pointed out, these Conventions reflect the principles of customary international law with respect to diplomatic and consular immunities and privileges. Because the privilege and immunities embodied in the Conventions have the force of international law they also have the force of common law in Canada to the extent the common law incorporates international law. Therefore, while the provisions of the Conventions do not have the force of statute law, a court would probably refer to them for guidance as to what is the customary diplomatic practice. The question which arises, however, is this: if the Vienna Conventions are already incorporated into Canadian law via the common law, why give certain of their articles the force of statute law?
I believe the bill really has its origin in the fact that the government of Quebec brought before the national assembly of that province in 1974 a bill dealing with the privileges and immunities of diplomatic and consular officials in that province, a bill which contained articles quite different from the principles embodied in the Vienna Conventions and one which was, in the opinion of federal government lawyers, outside the competence of the Quebec government. Quebec was duly
June 3, 1977

informed of this and a series of meetings was held on the subject between representatives of the two governments, the last one taking place early this year. The genesis of the bill before us lies, I suggest, in the action which was taken by Quebec.
As it happened, the legislation was not proceeded with following the election of a new government in Quebec which has not yet seen fit to seek legislative enactment of the provisions of the former bill. I believe this move on the part of Quebec caused the federal government to think seriously about this subject and it has apparently decided it would be highly desirable, if not necessary, to embody these diplomatic privileges and immunities in statute law as has been done in other common law countries.
Since the legislation does not represent a departure from previous practice there is no ground for our party objecting to it or delaying it. However, I do believe that certain questions as to the origins of the measure and the reason for bringing it forward at this time should be properly answered, hopefully in this Chamber before the conclusion of second reading or, if not, certainly at the committee stage. The legislation has a desirable consequence in that it states clearly and unequivocally the nature of the diplomatic immunities and privileges which Canada grants, and also the circumstances in which they may be suspended, revoked or reinstated.
The first question which needs to be asked is why certain articles in the Vienna Conventions have been left out. We have chosen to distinguish between those articles which establish rights and obligations between governments and which therefore do not require the force of law for implementation, and those articles which affect the rights of private persons in Canada or afford special privileges and immunities and which therefore do require the force of law for implementation. With this in mind, it is clear why certain articles were selected for inclusion while others were excluded, with the possible exception of Article 26 of the diplomatic convention which promises freedom of movement and travel anywhere in Canada, except for zones entering into which is restricted or regulated for reasons of national security.
This article was excluded from the list of articles to be incorporated into statute law. I think this raises a fundamental question which the minister should explain to us, even on second reading. According to external affairs, persons in Canada already have freedom to move in public places, and as this article neither affects this right nor specifies immunities or privileges, its inclusion was not considered to be necessary.
I think a fuller explanation is required, for members of some diplomatic missions do in fact have their freedom of movement limited. For example, we know that Soviet diplomats as well as Chinese diplomats in our city are restricted to an area within a certain radius of Ottawa. I think we might ask by what means these restrictions are imposed under present circumstances, and which diplomatic missions are so affected. Are these
Diplomatic Relations
restrictions to be regarded as a permanent feature of diplomatic relations between Canada and these other countries?
In other words, while it is true that Article 26 does not establish a privilege or an immunity, it is equally true that some diplomats do not enjoy normal freedom of movement in Canada. What we are seeking, therefore, is to establish why the principle of freedom of movement should not be included in the new statute.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, restriction of movement of foreign diplomats in Canada is a counter measure imposed by the Canadian government because the movement of Canadian diplomats in certain foreign countries is restricted. In essence, it is a tit for tat arrangement. Certain diplomats of various ranks from a foreign embassy are permitted to go a certain number of miles, which is all worked out on a sort of slide rule basis. I would only say that, as nations are coming closer together in a new kind of world which has grown up since the time the Vienna Conventions were first passed, more attention should be given on a universal basis to increasing all freedom of movement of diplomats in the countries to which they are properly accredited.
In saying that I am thinking, for example, of the restrictions which Canadian diplomats face in China, a country which I visited not so long ago, a reflection of which we find in today's Globe and Mail, in which a scientific team tells us about the effects of the recent earthquake in China which are only now coming to light because foreign diplomats and media personnel were not able to travel to the areas of China which suffered severely from the recent earthquake. Consequently the world at large had not realized the seriousness of the earthquake which struck China. Various measures of aid and assistance were withheld simply for lack of information. When I was in China Canadian authorities pointed out to me that they themselves could do a better job of reflecting the fullness of development inside China were they themselves able to travel more widely.
The same is true of Chinese diplomats who are accredited to Canada. The very idea that special permission is required for ranking members of the Chinese delegation in Ottawa to go out to the west coast or to my own province of Alberta is anathema to me, in the kind of world in which we live. Therefore I think it behooves the Canadian government to make an effort to increase the travel rights of all diplomats in nations to which they are accredited.
I move from considerations of travel to the final point that I want to make in my brief intervention. I refer to abuses of diplomatic privileges. I am going to say a word about Canada but I think I ought to put the matter in proper perspective. We read in a recent issue, March, 1977, The Economist of London that lawlessness is on the increase in Britain, if for no other reason than that the diplomatic community in London increasingly treats yellow lines in the streets as a bit of decoration to brighten the place up. The 32,000 parking tickets which were given to foreign diplomats in London in 1972 had grown last year to 93,000. The article gives a rather impressive list of
80016-57'/)

June 3, 1977
Diplomatic Relations
countries of the world which were ignoring traffic regulations in London.
We can now insert into the picture the Canadian experience. In 1975 some 5,516 foreign diplomats were accused of breaking Canadian laws but, of course, were not charged because they invoked diplomatic immunity. This is a situation which merits attention. The matter has been brought up in the House. Various spokesmen for the Department of External Affairs point out each time it is brought up that foreign diplomats ought to look to themselves to improve their record in the country which has received them, at the same time pointing out that when Canadian diplomats go abroad they are expected to respect the laws of the country which receives them, including the traffic laws. I dare say that any Canadian diplomat who ran up a record of traffic offences in the country which received him would not long be representing Canada. I think there is something out of balance here in the way that we tolerate such excessive violations of our laws under the guise of diplomatic immunity.
I have put on the record the 1975 figures. Let me give the 1976 figures for the city of Ottawa alone, which of course has the most diplomats in Canada. There were 4,788 traffic tickets issued to members of the diplomatic community in 1976. No charges were laid in connection with 13 traffic accidents and 82 traffic violations because diplomatic immunity was involved.
I think the external affairs department ought to be explaining in what way abuses of diplomatic status can be cut down. The country on the list with the highest number of infringements of Canadian law in which diplomatic immunity has been pleaded is Uganda, which topped the list of 1976 violations with 611.

speechtext:
It certainly is unacceptable, and I think it is also somewhat mysterious in view of the fact that there are only five accredited Ugandan diplomats in our city. This seems to suggest a gross violation of our laws by Ugandans, and I think it is time this country took some action.
In speaking of Uganda in terms of diplomatic immunity and the rights which representatives of countries have in other countries, all of which are encompassed in this bill, and at the same time considering the opening preamble to the Vienna Convention which talks of the promotion of friendly relations among nations, the principles of the United Nations and so on, 1 cannot conclude my remarks without insisting once more that we should seriously consider whether we should give hospitality to President Idi Amin of Uganda who stands a chance of getting into this country when the Commonwealth Games are held. I believe that the government ought to make very clear that we consider diplomatic niceties go only so far, that in the case of President Amin of Uganda no diplomatic niceties or courtesies will be extended, especially in light of the report of the International Commission of Jurists, a body which Ambassador Beaulne of Canada has said is beyond reproach.
[Mr. Roche.)
The International Commission of Jurists has reported to the United Nations, in a 130 page report, that 100,000 people have been murdered in the six years of Amin's administration. Therefore I think it is time for Canada to make very clear the limits of our tolerance.
I end with a quotation from the London Times concerning the report of the International Commission of Jurists. I refer to a quote from the Archbishop of Uganda who was murdered a few weeks ago in that country:
From the Archbishop to his own wife, President Amin knows no mercy. He kills, causes to be killed, presides over a growing apparatus for killing ...
The Organization of African Unity ignores the matter... The African states protect Amin from criticism in the United Nations. The United Nations Human Rights Commission is quite active in respect of South Africa, Chile and some other countries which its membership agree are inhumanely oppressive regimes. For the Human Rights Commission to live up to its title for a strong resolution, white men have to torment and debase black men or right wing secret police have to maltreat liberals or leftists. No other abrogation of human rights seems to produce any protest. In short, the Human Rights Commission has little or nothing to do with rights, justice or human conscience. It is, or has become, a political and propaganda body. It makes a mockery of human rights, as solemnly written into international conventions.
I conclude my comments on Bill C-6, bearing in mind that I think it is proper to raise a question as to the origin of the bill, to consider the travel restrictions, to talk about the abuses, and to focus once more on the special problem that Uganda presents to the diplomatic community today.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL CAMPAIGN TO PROMOTE HIGHWAY SAFETY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should initiate, in co-operation with provincial governments and appropriate organizations, a na-

June 3, 1977
Road Safety
tional campaign to promote driving safety throughout Canada in the interest of preservation of human life and courtesy among the driving public.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this week all hon. members of this House welcomed to this Chamber the six victors in the recent federal by-elections. Naturally not all of us were as pleased as they themselves or their respective parties must have been at those victories. Nevertheless, we all congratulate them, welcome them, and wish them well in their parliamentary careers.
Four of those members are new to this House and they will experience the unique feeling, or set of feelings, that only those who sit in this Chamber can possibly know. To sit in the House of Commons of Canada, knowing the confidence placed in you by your respective constituents, knowing of their high hopes and aspirations for our country, is to feel a very special bond with each and every Canadian citizen, and a heartfelt obligation to our wonderful country.
Every time that an hon. member rises to speak in this House, he is mindful of the tremendous privilege which has been given to him. I am certainly cognizant of that privilege every time I sit in this Chamber, especially when I have an opportunity to place before the House some thoughts of special concern to the people of Hamilton-Wentworth and, hopefully, to the people of Canada.
Therefore I appreciate the time and indulgence of the House in being here today and speaking very briefly in support of the motion which I have chosen as my one private member's motion of this session. Perhaps a word of background is in order.
During the last parliament I placed the very same motion before the consideration of this House, on April 29, 1974. Its fate was the one which seems to be common practice in this House, although I am happy to say it is a practice that seems to be growing less frequent, that is, the motion was debated until the allotted time had expired, and therefore no action was taken on the part of the government by virtue of a direction from this House, such as passage of the motion would have given.
During the debate, however, my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), spoke very briefly and said at that time, and 1 quote:
Regardless of what happens to the present motion raised in today's private members' hour, the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth has done a service by raising the issue. I join with him in calling for doubled and redoubled effort in all ways that can cut down the loss of life on our highways. I say to the hon. member that he has done well to raise this issue. I call on him to stick with it.
Those words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre meant a great deal to me, coming as they did from a gentleman who is recognized as one of the leading figures in this House. Obviously he and I have had our political disagreements, and continue to hold some very fundamental differences of opinion both in matters pertaining to political philosophy, current policies, and perhaps approaches to political life. But I have a respect for the hon. member which I believe to be shared in all parts of this House, and his comments to me
[Mr. O'Sullivan.j
during that last parliament, my First term in office, were a source of great encouragement and were very deeply appreciated. In this instance I am very happy indeed to take his advice. Moreover, the situation facing Canadians today in the matter of highway safety, driving safety generally, and courtesy on the roads still demands and commands the attention of the elected representatives of the Canadian people.
The motion is in many ways self-explanatory and does not require a great deal of elaboration beyond what it states quite simply. I call upon the federal government to initiate immediately, in co-operation with the provincial governments and appropriate organizations, a national campaign to promote driving safety throughout Canada in the interests of preservation of human life and courtesy among the driving public.
This is not to suggest that I should like to impose upon provincial governments a policy formulated here in Ottawa in an area which is clearly under the jurisdiction of those governments. The intent of this motion is, instead, to bring together the expertise which the provinces and the various safety-minded organizations in Canada have gathered through their own studies and research and driving safety campaigns. Quite simply, I want us to think as a nation in promoting driving safety, in combating the carnage on our highways. I believe that the Canadian people should have placed at their disposal the evidence and experience gained across the country so that we might benefit as a nation. I should just like to cite a couple of examples.
In 1975 the Ontario ministry of transportation and communications published "The Human Collision", which noted in part that during 1973 there were nearly 100,000 people injured and 2,000 killed in traffic accidents in Ontario. Serious accidents are especially frequent among younger people. For people under the age of 35, traffic accidents are responsible for more deaths than any disease and for more deaths than all other accidents combined. The booklet containing this information was prepared by the research and development division of the provincial ministry of transportation. The very existence of this division endorses my motion. It is but one agency studying traffic safety problems in one province. No doubt its aims and functions are duplicated over and over again. It is time to bring all that expertise together and, moreover, to present the details of the combined knowledge and research to the Canadian people.
Similarly, in 1974 the then minister of health and social development for Alberta established a task force on highway accidents and suicides. The Honourable Neil Crawford, who continues to have a distinguished career in provincial politics, belongs to a special fraternity of Canadians who have participated actively in the public life of Canada at various levels, having first gained their training in close association with one of the acknowledged masters of Canadian political life. I refer to those whose careers have included service as assistants on Parliament Hill to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). That special fraternity includes people as distinguished as Tom Van Dusen, Greg Guthrie, Lee Richard-
June 3, 1977

son, and most recently, Keith Martin, to name just a few of the prominent members of that group.
The document, or report, in 1974 to which I referred, was a concise and well-written document. There were a couple of points in it I thought noteworthy to the debate before us. The committee reported that they had assembled a collection of the world literature in their areas of interest and had accumulated a very large number of reference articles in both fields. I think it significant that this committee studying highway accidents should refer to world literature. It is a universal problem, and it seems to me that the important goal of protecting and saving human lives should encourage us to look beyond our limited borders, be they provincial or even national, to take full advantage of the experience of others.
This same interim report referred to a national roadside survey "which had been carried out in many Canadian provinces and which might serve as an opportunity for providing uniform information across the country". And the committee went on to say:
We feel that anything we could do to co-operate with the provinces and the Ministry of Transport to obtain information about situations on the highway would be worth while.
That we lack effective co-ordination of traffic procedures is clear. One need only look at the prevailing speed limits and statutes regulating seat belt legislation throughout the provinces as easy examples. The speeds vary, as do regulations pertaining to the wearing of seat belts. I do not wish to have this House, as I said earlier, impose its will upon provinces in an area under provincial jurisdiction, but we all share this common aim and goal of protecting the well-being and safety of Canadians. It falls to the federal government to take the initiative, to bring the provinces together, and to ensure that all Canadians benefit from the experience of individual provinces as well as from the expertise of safety minded organizations.
It would be improper on my part to suggest that no action has been taken in this area. In the same year that I first brought this motion to the attention of the House, the first meeting was held here in Ottawa of the officials participating in the federal-provincial co-operative road safety program. Its goal was to reduce the national road fatality rate by 15 per cent over five years. Just this past week a press release from Transport Canada arrived on my desk and I was delighted to note that in the period 1973 to 1976, a 30 per cent decrease in the national road fatality rate was reported at the most recent meeting of these same federal and provincial road safety officials. It is especially encouraging to quote some of the remarks contained in that press release. For example it states:
The number of highway fatalities in Canada dropped from 6,703 in 1973, an all time high, to 5,262 in 1976. This represents a decrease in the road fatality rate from 6.7 fatalities per million vehicle miles to 4.7, a 30 per cent reduction.
This downward trend in the number of fatalities, the first ever recorded in Canada's motoring history, occurred when the number of vehicles and the amount of travel on Canadian highways was increasing.
Road Safety
The federal and provincial representatives recognized that the decrease has likely been influenced by changes in economic and social conditions in recent years, as well as by various federal and provincial measures under the co-operative program.
Nothing could have pleased me more than to read that information from Transport Canada, and I wish to take this opportunity to express, I am confident, on behalf of all members of this House, and all drivers in Canada, deep-felt appreciation to those responsible for bringing about this federal-provincial co-operative road safety program, and for the co-operation obviously extended in its tremendous success. It has brought us closer to our goal, but we are still 5,206 human lives away from our ultimate goal and aim, and many tens of thousands of human injuries away.
Looking ahead, therefore, I want the House, through my motion, to commend and endorse this program so strongly that it will continue, and will be given the fullest possible support by this government and by all provincial governments and safety-minded agencies so that the co-operative program will continue in the coming years, as has been promised.
What sort of national campaign do I want to see brought about? I shall leave the details to those far better versed than I in this special area. But I think that any campaign of promoting driving courtesy, which ultimately results in greater safety on the roads, must, to be successful, be a joint venture that has the support of Canadian governments at all levels, and one that is realistic in its approach to the problem.
We are all aware that the dangers on the road are especially severe in so far as young people are concerned, and statistics indicate that young male drivers are the most frequent victims. Any national campaign to promote driving safety would be off to a good start if it heeded the advice of Mr. J. Lome McDougall, a former professor and member of the city council of Kingston, who wrote an article published in the Calgary Herald on March 3, 1977. He contrasted the traditional approach of promoting driving safety with the one which he believes, and I share his view, would have much greater success. I quote Mr. McDougall:
The well-intentioned old want to save young men from themselves. If they are to be successful, they must learn to invite co-operation, and win it, or they will get nowhere.
Maybe it would help if they would start by trying to state the positive values they wish the young to adopt. They might even learn something about themselves if they would do so.
Forget the prohibitions; they get nowhere. Try being positive.
See if you can promote respect for life (including one's own), courtesy, and consideration for the right of others.
From there it is a small step to asking the young to grow in self-respect, and once that point is made, many good things may follow.
Speak with the voice of force and compulsion and you will speak to deaf ears.
Invite a discussion of the moral problem and young men may hear you.
That is wise advice form Mr. McDougall which I commend to all officials should they decide to accept the challenge that I hope this House will endorse, of bringing about a great national campaign, supported by governments at all levels, to promote driving safety and courtesy.

June 3, 1977
Road Safety
It is only natural, Mr. Speaker, that I would be grateful if this House should decide to endorse my motion.
I have already taken note of, and expressed commendation for, the actions already taken by both federal and provincial officials in this field. The adoption of my resolution today would, in my opinion, serve the useful purpose of encouraging those officials to continue and expand their efforts.
The purpose of this motion is quite simple. We, as members of parliament, are sent here by the Canadian people to preserve their freedoms and protect their rights. The most basic right is	that of life itself.	That is why I introduced	this motionin the	last parliament	and have	now brought	it forwardagain at this time. Much has been done. But, as the families of traffic victims will attest, there is much that remains for all of us to do. The protection of this very basic right, the right to life, is	surely one of the greatest	concerns and	one of thehighest	causes to which	a member	of parliament	can devote
whatever time he or she may be privileged to serve in this House.
Many hon. members have, in their own way, advanced and defended this great right, this basic right, of all the Canadian people. I think, for example, that by her courageous action the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) has taken great political risks, especially in standing up to very powerful figures within her own party, in her own very dedicated efforts to advance the preservation and protection of human life at all its stages. I cite her as an example of outstanding dedication and moral courage to those new members to whom I referred earlier, and who have joined us in this Chamber in this House of Commons this past week.
As one who came to parliament in 1972, with the same high hopes and the same aspirations as, no doubt, the new members bring, I want to pass along this brief word of advice. Nothing could honour their careers in this place more that to take an active role, whenever the opportunity arises, in advancing the cause of the most basic right and freedom of every Canadian, the right to life.
Perhaps all of us who sit in this House, regardless of the seniority or official opposition given to us, might reflect upon this essential duty of every member of parliament. In thinking about it, in thinking about our duties and reflecting upon our role as the elected representatives of the people of Canada, I recalled a letter which I received in 1966 when I was 14 years old, a student in Hamilton, and very much interested in policital life. I had already been a member of the Progressive Conservative party for two years, having since the age of 12 taken an active part in politics at various levels. I am mindful of the very special opportunities which have been given to me and am deeply grateful to that party and to the people who have made all of them possible. I think of the unique experience which has been mine, such as twice being elected from Hamilton-Wentworth under the leadership of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield).
I think, as well, that now I am serving in this House, at a time probably more exciting and important than any time in our history, with the possible exception of Confederation,

under the leadership of the dedicated Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), with whom I entered parliament in 1972, and whose compassion, concern, and qualities of leadership are known to all in this House. Moreover, I reflect upon the wonderful experience which was mine prior to election to parliament in serving as executive assistant to the right hon. member for Prince Albert, the person who brought me into political life.
The words which he spoke in this House, and which were contained in his letter to me dated April 4, 1976, reflect an attitude of parliament that I believe would be shared by both party leaders whom 1 have just mentioned, and with whom I share an esteem for the Dean of this House. Although it is not my practice to make public use of personal correspondence, I believe that he would not mind being quoted in that letter which reads in part as follows:
I was interested in your comment on the recent events in parliament, and I am sure that you will be in full agreement with the words I used during the debate to which you refer:
"Mr. Speaker, this institution must not fail. Without it there is no freedom. We are here today not only as the custodians of the present and inheritors of the past but, Mr. Speaker, we are as well the hope of this institution's future. Let us get to work on the many issues facing Canada today."
It is signed, of course, by the right hon. member for Prince Albert. I fully agree with those comments. I hope all hon. members will take them to heart as we pause to recall what a tremendous honour and privilege it is to serve the Canadian people in this House of Commons, and especially to work with people such as the right hon. member.
I am grateful to the House for the time given to me to present this motion, and at this time I too say in a non-partisan spirit, starting with this motion of vital importance concerning human life, this institution must not fail. Let us get to work on the many issues facing Canada today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) for proposing the motion we are dealing with today, and particularly for the very excellent speech he just gave to the House. Every time he speaks I enjoy listening to him. Whether 1 agree with him or not, I appreciate the sincerity with which he delivers his speeches, and also his ability. I think he makes a real contribution to the Parliament of Canada.
The hon. member has proposed this motion previously, and I agree with him that those who succeed with points of view in this House are those who raise them often and speak to them strongly. Perhaps by doing that the hon. member will achieve his objective.
Surely all hon. members share the concern of the hon. member. In 1973 traffic fatalities reached an all-time high of well over 6,700 people, which is very high when it is considered as a percentage of the Canadian population. Early in 1974 a joint statement released by the federal and provincial ministers
June 3, 1977

responsible for road safety and motor vehicle administration indicated the intention of those ministers to increase safety efforts and to establish a five-year program to improve the road safety situation.
A target reduction of 15 per cent in the traffic fatality rate by 1979 was set. In view of the rapidly increasing number of cars on the road those ministers were very optimistic to think that they could achieve such a goal, but I am pleased to report, as did the previous speaker, that not only has that goal been met, but it has actually been exceeded. In a statement which was issued recently by Transport Canada-I believe last week following the most recent series of meetings of senior officials from the 11 governments-it was noted that fatalities had fallen from 5,262 to a rate of 4.7 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles driven. This represents a decrease in the fatality rate of 30 per cent since 1973. I do not think any one person or group can take most of the credit; that credit should be shared amongst the many people who have been concerned about this problem and who have done something about it.
Many factors have been involved, not the least of which, I suggest, was the emergence of the energy situation. Perhaps people are now driving fewer miles per person than they were previously, and hopefully they are driving the miles they do drive at a lower rate of speed in an effort not only to reduce the number of deaths on our highways but also to achieve greater energy efficiency from their cars.
The same statement identified a number of measures which have contributed to this decrease, in addition to those I mentioned. Improved seat belts and increased public awareness of the benefits of them have contributed to the decrease. Two provinces have passed legislation requiring the use of seat belts. 1 think that has been an important factor. Certainly in the late model cars 1 have driven the seat belts are much more comfortable and more convenient than those used in the past. In my own case, I use them much more than I did previously because seat belts in the past were neither convenient nor particularly comfortable.
I have heard comments from a number of women suggesting that the seat belts in older cars are very uncomfortable for them to use. I think the improvement in the design has meant that many more travelling Canadians now use seat belts. That has obviously contributed to the better road safety record we now enjoy.
We now have stiffer penalties in the Criminal Code for impaired driving. Some of those penalties have been debated in this House during the life of this parliament. Speed limits have been reduced in several provinces. That has been beneficial, but certainly not to the degree it could be. The lowering of the speed limits coincided with concern about energy supplies, yet when one travels on our highways the fact that the speed limits have been reduced is not terribly apparent.
That is not the impression one gets when travelling in the United States. Where speed limits are 55 miles an hour in the United States, that is the rate of speed of most of the traffic. I suggest that on many of the highways in Canada the majority of drivers exceed the speed limit, and a great deal of highway
Road Safety
safety could be achieved by an even more rigorous policing of our reduced speed limits.
There has been a systematic removal of road hazards and continued improvement in highway design. I was driving on quite an old highway last week, and I thought about how safe our newer highways are in comparison. That is perhaps one of the things we often overlook. The highways in many parts of Canada have wide shoulders and fairly well designed and banked turns. There are adequate signs to indicate hazards and so on, and perhaps all those things have been very effective as well. Many organizations have initiated programs which weigh on the consciences of people, and that has been effective. I have been impressed by television advertising, particularly that of the Ministry of Transport, in relation to impaired driving. Those advertisements are perhaps the most effective I have seen with regard to almost anything, and perhaps that message is slowly getting across.
As a result of the efforts of the Canadian Safety Council, the automobile industry and the provinces, there has been a good deal of promotional material on the safer use of motor vehicles and also on the training of people who use them. Being an engineer, I am interested in design, and while many people complain that we do not build cars the way we used to, perhaps from a safety point of view it is a good thing we do not because new cars today are certainly much safer than those which were built 10, 12 or 15 years ago. I think that public concern that automobiles are built safely is demonstrated by the number of recalls which take place. It takes very little concern about the safety of motor products to get manufacturers to go to considerable expense and trouble to recall vehicles with inadequacies. I think that is a very commendable thing.
I wanted to participate briefly in this debate to indicate that a good deal has been accomplished but, as the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth indicated, it is only a start. I congratulate him on his statement. We are still exceeding our goal by some 5,000 deaths and we want to strive for a totally fatality-free record of driving in Canada. I hope that all levels of government, voluntary organizations, and all the people concerned, will make a co-ordinated effort to achieve this worth-while goal.

It is fine to have laws that provide penalties for impaired driving and so on, but I think we must go further than that and support the kind of campaign that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) sometimes engages in which would call for a changed attitude toward the drinking of alcoholic beverages.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to respond to the motion proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) I want to add my commendation for his persistence. As the member for the neighbouring riding I am well aware of his persistence and hard work.
I would stress the seriousness of the road safety problem, if I may, by making a comparison to the costs of World War II not only in dollars but in terms of human lives and suffering. During six years of war, total Canadian military appropriations were $11.6 billion dollars, or an average of $1.93 billion per year. In 1975 the costs to our country in terms of medical bills, car repairs, and loss of productivity as a result of traffic

accidents was estimated to be 2 per cent of the Gross National Product, or $2.5 billion. There were 17,682 Canadian battle deaths or persons who died of battle injuries over the six-year period of the war, an average of 2,950 fatalities per year. In comparison there have been 36,113 traffic fatalities in the last six years, or an average of 6,000 per year. These appallingly gross figures attest to the need for a co-ordinated effort by all levels of government in implementing a multi-disciplinary countermeasures program to combat the road safety problem.
Recent accident investigations estimate that 80 per cent to 90 per cent of traffic accidents are a result of human error. It is my opinion, and I am sure this opinion is shared by others, and it was alluded to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that a major source of that error is alcohol, with 40 per cent of drivers killed being found impaired, and 53 per cent of adult pedestrians killed being found impaired, as well. In view of these figures, Mr. Speaker, I will confine my remarks to the Canadian government's research activities and countermeasures programs relating to the problem of impaired driving and the role of alcohol in traffic accidents.
In 1974 Transport Canada conducted a national roadside survey, using an internationally approved methodology, in order to assess the nature and extent of drinking and driving habits in Canada. During a 12-week period 9,700 drivers were surveyed at over 500 sites across Canada between the hours of 10 p.m. and 3 a.m. on Wednesday, Thursday, and Saturday nights. Information on drinking habits, trip origin and destination, as well as demographic information, was collected. In addition, each driver was asked to provide a sample of breath which was later analyzed for blood alcohol content.
Of the drivers surveyed 20.4 per cent had been drinking prior to driving, 11.2 per cent were probably impaired, and 5.4 per cent had blood alcohol concentration at or above the statutory limit of 80 mg per cent. The results of this survey indicate that the chance of meeting a drinking driver more than doubles between the two hours prior to midnight and the 1 a.m. to 3 a.m. time period. Drinking and driving appears to be almost as serious on weekdays as on week ends. The data also reveals that driving after drinking is most prevalent among males, among the middle-aged, among the unemployed, and among the separated and divorced drivers.
I point out that a survey of this nature is important, in that it provides an excellent data base against which comparisons of fatality data for the same population can be made; it also provides us with considerable knowledge about the Canadian public's drinking and driving behavior. Public education campaigns and/or changes in impaired driving legislation can thus be evaluated for effectiveness if we have clearly defined the extent and nature of the problem prior to our particular counter measures program.
As an example of the first use, a non-governmental traffic safety conscious agency was able to compare 1973 driver fatality data for five provinces with the government's national
June 3, 1977

roadside survey exposure data in a collaborative effort, to determine if impaired drivers in certain age groups are over represented in driver fatalities. As a result of this comparison we now know that impaired drivers 16 to 17 years old face a terrible risk on the roads in that they are 165 times as likely to die in an automobile accident as the average non-impaired driver. Youths 18 to 19 years old are 70 times as likely to become fatality statistics when driving impaired. Other persons driving with a relatively high risk when impaired are the 50 year olds and above. They are 39 times as likely to die in a traffic accident when driving impaired, compared to the average non-impaired driver.
The age group with the lowest risk of fatality appears to be the 30 to 34 year olds, but even impaired drivers within this age category are 17 times as likely to be fatally injured in a road accident. Suffice it to say that drivers of all ages are at considerably greater risk of being killed when driving impaired than when driving sober.
One area in which the Canadian government has concerned itself with changing people's attitudes and behavior with respect to drinking and driving is in strict impaired driving legislation. I am pleased to report that further information gathered on the effect of the 1969 breathalizer legislation indicates a drop in traffic fatalities immediately subsequent to its passage. Recently, however, traffic fatality figures have risen, especially for very young drivers. This increase was originally attributed to the lowering of the age of majority between 1970 and 1972 in the various provinces. Recent evidence from a study conducted by the Traffic Injury Research Foundation suggests that the lowering of the drinking age had no substantial impact on this increase in young driver deaths in the provinces studied. Rather the authors more properly attributed the increase to the "rebound" effects of the ".08" legislation in Canada; that is, the impaired driving legislation of 1969 is believed to be less effective now in deterring impaired driving than it was just subsequent to passage.
With this in mind, in January, 1976, when the provisions of Bill C-71 were agreed upon in this House, amendments were made to the legislation which we feel will aid police officers in detecting impaired drivers on the road and result in more fines and convictions for the various Criminal Code offences. Specifically provision was made in the code for roadside breath testing involving the use of a portable device capable of detecting the presence of alcohol on the breath of an apprehended driver. Peace officers can now stop drivers whom they suspect may have been drinking. Previously, law enforcers were restricted by the law to pulling over only those drivers suspected of impairment. That you may argue, is a subtle distinction, but this "reasonable cause" provision should enable peace officers to detect more easily those drivers potentially dangerous to themselves and others, regardless of whether their driving behavior is erratic.
Since before these changes were made a blood alcohol concentration of impaired drivers on average was 170 mg. per cent, or more than twice the statutory limit, the old legislation
Road Safety
was regarded as inadequate for the detection of those drivers at or just above the 80 mg. per cent limit. Not only should the new legislation increase the likelihood of detection, but fines and jail terms have been increased as well which should act as further deterrents. It is up to respective provincial governments to proclaim these laws in force, and up to both provincial and municipal authorities to ensure enforcement of the new legislation.
In order to increase the Canadian public's awareness of these legislative changes the Department of Transport has concerned itself with educating Canadians through public information campaigns designed to inform the public of the seriousness of the alcohol and road safety problem. To this end an information package has been developed, consisting of television, radio and newspaper advertisements, an audiovisual slide presentation, a leaflet which contains the major points outlined in the audio-visual presentation, and an information booklet on alcohol and drinking drivers. This information package was made available in February, 1977, to various traffic safety conscious groups across Canada, to be used in conjunction with on-going community programs.
As hon. members can see, we have made changes, have made representations, and have met with success. We are still trying to reduce the figures the hon. member mentioned to lower levels, preferably to zero. I emphasize again the seriousness of the drinking driver problem. Though 1 represent Canada's grape and wine country, I insist that alcohol and driving do not go together.

I have found the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth to be a most honest, forthright, and dedicated young man, dedicated to proper principles with which this House ought to be associated. He has shown an honest desire to serve the people of his riding and the people of Canada to the best of his ability.
I am glad we are debating this motion. I think we can serve the ends of the motion by discussing its subject matter on the floor of the House of Commons. We have only one hour available for the discussion. I wish a day were available for the discussion of these vital aspects of highway safety. A great deal hinges on effective highway safety measures.
Hon. members have mentioned areas in which improvement has taken place. The hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) told the House of improvements which have been made in road building, following discussions with provinces and manufacturers. The hon. member who just resumed his
80016-58 Zi

June 3, 1977
Road Safety
seat spoke of the serious problem of the drinking driver, of young, middle aged and older drivers, and showed how vulnerable are young drinking drivers.
To those hon. members present in this House during this late hour on a Friday afternoon, I wish to speak as a parent and concerned individual who has been deeply associated for many years with some of the questions we are discussing. Before I was elected to this House I had pursued a somewhat varied career, as news editor of a television station, and as a peace officer in Ontario. I can tell you that if there is one thing a police officer hates to investigate it is an accident involving young people. When I say this I note the presence of young people in our galleries. We must involve mothers and fathers and young people in our discussion, for we are discussing a most serious subject, one which can affect lives.
As the hon. member who just resumed his seat said, drinking and driving do not mix. I say to our parents and older people, and to your young people, if they fail to use their seat belts when driving in automobiles they can endanger their own lives. Young and new drivers must be properly educated to the hazards of the road. Although nobody has mentioned it today, one of the important steps taken in the last few years for increasing driver awareness of road hazards is the introduction of school driving courses. Most young drivers in Ontario now find themselves subjected to such courses.
In investigating many of the accidents it was my misfortune to investigate from time to time, I found very often that they involved a young person who had made one mistake. It is that one mistake which we must eliminate. It is that one moment of carelessness while at the wheel of a car. It is that one moment while enjoying good friends and good times, when they fail to realize that that "one last drink"may be just the one last drink that is needed to get them and their friends, and other people they may never have met before, into a situation where death and destruction can result in the flicker of an eyelash.
I am not sure that if we were to complete our discussion and finish our debate on this important subject this afternoon we would really be doing the hon. member for Hamilton-Went-worth the best of favours. I hope, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, that his persistence in introducing this subject for discussion is rewarded. It may come up only once a year, but it is important that all members use these few moments in which to put forward their honest views to show those who are in the press gallery, and others who are with us late on a Friday afternoon, that we are concerned about this important matter.
There has been increased consultation, as the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth mentioned, through the federal-provincial road safety co-operatives. This will be continued. Compulsory use of safety belts has been introduced in the last two years and this has significantly reduced the number of highway fatalities in those provinces where the use of seat belts has become mandatory. Many departments integrate their thinking on the question of safety, including the Ministry of Health,

the Ministry of Transport, the Department of the Solicitor General, and the Department of Justice. Individual and group efforts along these lines must continue so as to place before the people the importance of the motion which has been presented to us today.
I believe we must also look to more and better public transit as an element which will relieve congestion on our highways in and around the large cities. It is during the rush-hour that many of the more serious accidents take place. Recently it was my pleasure to visit Germany. Their most serious accidents occur on well-constructed four-lane highways when a heavy congestion of traffic is moving at relatively high speeds. Our own traffic acts provide for legal speeds of 55 miles per hour. In Germany the speed of traffic is almost unlimited on some of the super highways. I believe the provinces have done a considerable service to the driving public and Canadians in general by reducing the permitted speed to the 55 mph mark in most cases.
The recent introduction by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) of the mandatory breathalyzer concept and the introduction of a system of spot-checks in conjunction with the provincial solicitors general are important steps forward which will give the police forces throughout this country a handle on a very dangerous situation caused by the actions of impaired drivers who would normally go unnoticed and who could not legally be subjected to that type of test.
There are many other things I would like to have said, Mr. Speaker, but I know other members wish to contribute to the debate. I thank the hon. member for putting forward this motion. It is by this type of debate and publicity that the House can best serve the needs and aspirations of the public in promoting safe driving.
